sections.heading: When it fits
sections.content: In response to a question about product-led, growth-oriented, freemium products, Camille agrees, then broadens the fit: community is useful when organic growth would benefit the company, or when limited resources, team capacity, or difficulty with paid growth make cracking organic growth important. She says that organic flywheel can later buttress paid growth.

sections.content: She cautions that community is not right for every company. More sales-led products—often pricier products or those with longer contracts—may call for a different approach; community need not mean a large forum, and the right initiative depends on the company’s context.

sections.heading: Strong fit
sections.content: When asked whether community is especially effective for product-led, growth-oriented freemium products, Ricketts agreed and broadened the point: it can work well when organic growth would be beneficial, or when a company needs to crack organic growth because it lacks the resources or team for paid growth. She described community as a buttress for paid growth the company may pursue later.

sections.heading: Why it can help—and a caveat
sections.content: At Notion, Ricketts defined community-led growth as building enough ubiquity and name recognition to help move upmarket into enterprise. But she cautioned that community does not have to mean a large forum, and its form should fit the company: sales-led products that are pricier or involve longer contracts may be a less natural fit for the same approach, while still benefiting from other community-related initiatives.

answer.summary: Ricketts says community-led growth is especially useful for product-led, often freemium products where organic growth matters—or where a company needs to build an organic growth engine because paid growth is constrained. It can complement paid growth later, and community can also help products gain recognition and move upmarket.

sections.heading: Best-fit products
sections.content: She broadly agrees that product-led, growth-oriented freemium products are a good fit, then widens the criterion: community can be valuable whenever organic growth would benefit the company, especially if limited resources or team capacity make paid growth difficult to rely on. An organic flywheel can later support paid growth rather than replace it.

sections.heading: Why it can work—and a caveat
sections.content: At Notion, community-generated sharing and word of mouth helped build ubiquity and name recognition, which reduced the risk companies perceived in choosing the product and supported expansion into larger teams and enterprise. Ricketts also notes that pricier products with longer contracts and a more sales-led culture may be a less obvious fit for heavy community investment—but community need not mean a large chat forum; the right form depends on the product and its stage.
